michigan.headline: What we learned after Michigan Football’s loss to MSU: We’ve hit rock bottom
michigan.body:
Saturday was the culmination of everything wrong with the Michigan football program in 2026. As the 2-6 Michigan State Spartans hooped and hollered around The Big House, carrying Paul Bunyan with them after a 15-6 victory over their in-state rivals, there was nothing first-year head coach Kyle Whittingham could do except say, “I can’t explain what just happened.”

Here’s what we learned about this team and the program after one of the most unacceptable losses in the program’s history.

This program just hit rock bottom

An offseason full of turmoil should have been the worst thing that happened for the program. Embarrassment in that moment was an understatement from a culture and values perspective. The one thing that fans and the administration could lean on was young talent on the field, despite a team that missed expectations for the second year in a row.

Warde Manuel, the athletic department and the university’s administration had the chance to stop the bleeding. A full turnaround of the Michigan culture was necessary, but with the talent at their disposal, returning to relevance should have been quick.

From the moment Whittingham entered the building, this team has been in free fall. From being a Hail Mary away from losing to Western Michigan to the loss to Michigan State, this team has progressively gotten worse throughout the season.

The Spartans already were not a good team, going winless in the Big Ten up until Saturday. But they were also down four starters on the defensive side of the ball and lost several more contributors throughout the game. Michigan accounted for only 192 total yards and turned the ball over four times against that limping defense, and 75 of those yards came on a garbage-time drive, saving the Wolverines from being shut out in The Big House.

From the five-star quarterback this coaching staff benched to make him the scapegoat for their offensive woes, to the five-star freshman running back who astonishingly had seven touches in Saturday’s game, to captain Jordan Marshall who inexplicably has seven carries over the last two games, it’s hard to put into words how discombobulated this offense is. There are about a dozen good-to-great players on that side of the ball who put misguided trust in Whittingham and Jason Beck, and wasted a valuable year of eligibility because of it.

Animosity from the locker room already leaked last month when Zack Marshall’s texts leaked on social media. After Saturday, there’s no way his thoughts are isolated. Michigan’s fallen to the bottom-15 in the country in yards and points per game, all while averaging almost two turnovers per game.

Then there’s the paradigm in the locker room with the defense because as good as it is. According to the Josh Dubow of the AP, Michigan is the 15th team in the last 15 seasons to allow 21 points or less in each of the first nine games of a season. The other 14 teams went a combined 119-7, while Michigan sits at 5-4.

What might be the craziest part is Whittingham already knows what this is going to cost the team. “We’ll probably be 50 percent new guys next year,” he said two weeks ago. Statements like this aren’t made unless you already feel a sense of losing control.

Now comes a significant challenge, as Michigan has three ranked opponents remaining. This team is full of players with nothing to compete for, and a football program with potentially a lame duck offensive coordinator and head coach, along with changes coming at athletic director and university president. It begs the question: who even does make the decisions about the football program’s leadership today?

A group of college athletes who also likely have one foot out the door now has to rally to beat one of Oregon, UCLA or Ohio State to make a bowl game. With the energy around this team following one of the worst losses in program history, the likelihood of that happening feels infinitesimal. But hey, at least there are no trophies left in those three games, right?

Kyle Whittingham on keeping Michigan motivated for its last 3 games:

"It's my job as a coach to rally them back up and get them ready to compete for these last three games. … I don't know, are there any more trophies in these last three games? I don't think there's any more… pic.twitter.com/9xkxiLp6Ih
— Anthony Broome (@anthonytbroome) November 8, 2026

michigan.headline: Burning Bridge: Michigan Football needs to start planning for a future without Kyle Whittingham
michigan.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham looks up at the scoreboard during second half action at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Michigan State won the game 15-6. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Over the offseason, excitement built steadily for the 2026 Michigan football season. There were plenty of reasons for optimism with Kyle Whittingham coming in to take over the program. One of the winningest coaches of the 21st century was finally getting the chance to prove himself in a place that’s well-resourced and always has a stream of talent.

Instead, the fan base had the wool pulled over its eyes, Michigan’s administration got duped, and the program sits in as bad a place as it’s been since the turn of the century.

The idea of hiring Whittingham made a lot of sense last December. Rocked by scandals over the last few years, Michigan needed someone who could stabilize things and be an “adult in the room” while also bringing in enough football acumen to help turn a talented roster into a winner in short order.

The “short order” part is key due to Whittingham’s age. At 66, it was clear he’d be in Ann Arbor for only a few years before finally retiring, giving it one last shot to go for a national title. With as much talent as Michigan already had on its roster and the nine wins it had in 2025, no ramp-up was needed. But instead, the team has taken several steps back and looks nowhere close to where it was even at this time last year.

This has been most evident over Michigan’s last two games: a sleepy seven-point win at Rutgers, and Saturday’s debacle in which the Wolverines looked totally uninspired and unprepared against a 3-6 Michigan State team. There are three games left, but it’s apparent Michigan has mailed it in, with three more losses surely coming.

Michigan’s season going off the rails like this is unfathomable if you think about how much optimism there was just three months ago and how many good pieces were in place. However, it’s not a total surprise if you’ve watched college football for any length of time. There have been plenty of teams that come into the year in similar situations with good rosters and coaching staffs only to see that optimism dwindle at the first signs of adversity.

Perhaps this has been amplified over the last few years, with the portal bringing together teams full of players who don’t have deep ties to one another and less loyalty to their schools than ever before. Programs like Florida State, Texas A&M, Penn State, Oklahoma, Clemson and Florida have all had major expectations in recent years and seen their seasons go down in flames by mid-October, with Michigan joining them this season.

While the Wolverines certainly belong on that list of programs that have fallen from grace, they’re also a bit of an outlier, having won a national championship just three years ago. They also don’t have a young head coach who’s simply going through growing pains — they have someone who was supposed to be the answer, but he has only dragged them further away from success and clearly doesn’t understand or respect the position he’s in.

At this point, we’ve seen enough to know nothing is going to happen in the next three games or over the next calendar year to make the future outlook better. The aforementioned programs like Florida State have gotten a jump on things by firing Mike Norvell — even with a big buyout — because they understand there’s no sense in continuing to trot out a sub-standard product. The future interests of the program need to be at the top of mind, especially when there’s nothing going on in the present that inspires any hope.

Whittingham was only ever viewed as a bridge option to the next head coach who might be able to have some success in the meantime. But this bridge is clearly burning, and Michigan needs to start looking to the future before it digs itself an even deeper hole.

michigan.headline: Michigan Football reaches new low on ESPN FPI rankings after loss to MSU

And just like that, offensive coordinator Jason Beck is gone, Michigan Football (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) has fallen to two games below .500 in conference play, and the ESPN FPI Rankings are not impressed with the Wolverines.

Michigan came in at 38th nationally after Saturday’s loss, with an Index score of 9.1 — the 11th best among Big Ten teams.

Bowl eligibility still seems reasonable; the FPI projects 5.8 wins for the Wolverines. However, with No. 5 Ohio State (24.5), No. 9 Oregon (19.7) and No. 27 UCLA (12.6) remaining on the schedule, this season could very well end this month.

The Wolverines are given just a 1.0 percent chance of winning out and a 63.1 percent likelihood of reaching that six-win mark to make the postseason. The odds haven’t been in their favor for most of the season, and the loss to Michigan State over the weekend only made those chances even worse.

Is there anything left to look forward to with this team? Or have you given up and already started to think about 2027? Let us know down in the comments section below.

michigan.headline: Best and Worst:  MSU
michigan.body:
Best and Worst:  MSU
bronxblue
November 8th, 2026 at 10:58 PM

Best? Worst?: Plot Twist!

I wrote about half of this diary before news of Jason Beck's firing was announced, and because (a) I still think a lot of the complaints I have about the offense are more holistic and unlikely to shift dramatically with Harding now serving as OC, and (b) it's a free blog so it can be whatever length I want, I'm keeping most of it. But if you notice some shifts in tone just be forwarned.
In terms of Beck being relieved of his duties and how I feel that impacts the season, it's both too late and unlikely to be meaningfully impactful. This disastrous preseason install doomed the team from the jump, and while a change during the bye week maybe would have helped at the margins the minute they benched Bryce Underwood and then intimated through certain channels that he was the one holding the offense back there was no real chance for salvation. And despite some faint scents of hopium wafting through the Michigan parts of the internet, Harding hasn't served as an offensive coordinator since 2016 at Utah (and that was as a co-OC with current BYU OC Aaron Roderick) and those offenses were...fine but about where UM's 2024 offense finished. You know, the offense that featured Alex Orji, Davis Warren, Jack Tuttle at QB and barely completed 60% of its passes and had more picks than TDs.
Now, given how well the defense has played thus far and the state of the B1G, an offense of that caliber to start the year probably puts Michigan at 8-1 heading into this home stretch, but with 3 games to go I have my doubts the guy whose offensive line looks like they're learning blocking from YouTube clips in between drives is going to do much. This probably ups the chances of the team pulling off an upset against UCLA, Oregon, or OSU marginally but there isn't enough lipstick in a Sephora to pretty up this offensive pig, and regardless of what happens going forward it should not change the fact that Whittingham needs to be thrown out of this job the minute a new AD is announced. But hey, at least the last 3 games won't be fully depressing affairs because at the very least we're promised a different type of car wreck than we've gotten thus far.
Worst: Just Don't Care

Normally I'd be more upset about a loss to MSU but I'm mostly annoyed than anything else. Pat Fitzgerald just seems like a cretin, an asshole who acts like a Builder of Men but who apparently didn't notice a bunch of his players were sexually assaulting each other for years. He's been vocally against player movement and empowerment for years. Oh, and in his last 3 non-COVID years at NW he went a combined 7-29 with progressively worse teams.
To lose to him as MSU's coach makes the loss sting because, honestly, I don't otherwise have much animosity toward MSU. They suck just like UM, they've been ravaged by injuries in ways that make me sympathetic, and they're sort of stuck in no-man's land in the new CFB hierarchy because they don't have a ton of money and they're fighting with the basketball team for it. Their ceiling looks like 6-7 wins most years, with middling talent and a chance to sometimes be a spoiler. Their players didn't try to beat Michigan's players with helmets, or crank their necks in piles, or do anything nefarious. There was some pushing and shoving but nothing got out of hand, and if you swapped out the MSU jerseys for, say, NW's I don't think anyone would have noticed on the field. So in a season where UM has already lost the Jug as well as to Iowa, losing Bunyan to a garbage MSU team just doesn't get me worked up all that much. I'm sure that'll change the next time a football season matters, but not this year.
Worst: A Single Game
I've noted previously that I listen a decent number of podcasts, and one of my favorite ones is called If Books Could Kill, a podcast that analyzes the Ted Talk/Self Help/Airport non-fiction genre. The hosts reads books like Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, Rich Dad Poor Dad, and Freakanomics, dig into the data/concepts underpinning the works, and usually come to the conclusion that the core concepts are either dubiously extrapolated from small data sets, not nearly as universal as the authors claim, or sometimes just made up.
Over the years they've seen this pattern of lazy data interpretation, the mixing of correlation with causation, and snake-oil sales across enough novels and authors that they've come up with the One Book Theory. Basically, all these books have the same basic structure and the same general lessons - X happens because of Y, you can overcome/exploit it with Z, boring stuff already proven by experts is regurgitated but with a bit more pizzazz - and so if you've read one you've basically read them all. Just take the general vibes you already have, change the names, dates, and circumstances, and you've got the gist of any other book. Saves you time and money.
Well, every game this year save maybe UTEP has felt like the same game. Michigan's offense struggles to establish the run or move the ball in chunks, the opposing defense knows what's coming so they tee off, and the defense valiantly tries to keep them in it until a turnover or an errant breakdown by the opponent helps UM score some points. If one or two things more break for UM over their opponent, they win by 1 score; otherwise they lose by a similar margin. Michigan sits at 5-4 on the year and unsurprisingly are 4-3 in 1-score games, 4-and-4 if you allow that the MSU game would have been an 8-point loss had Whittingham kicked after the TD. Again, ignoring UTEP Michigan has a point differential of -5, which is some real Nebraska-under-Scott-Frost remixing. If you've seen one Michigan game this year you've basically seen them all, and while I love a sequel at some point you can tell the writers have run out of ideas.
Sadly, there's little evidence this is going to change going forward. Even if Beck makes adjustments in scheme or personnel, it's unlikely the offense will meaningfully change. And if anything, the defense is likely to get worse as they are further left out to dry by the offense and opponents have more time to scout and adjust. If there was a way to sim to the end of the season now, my guess is a lot of UM fans would take it.
Worst: No Weird Trick
The other big takeaway from the If Books Could Kill podcast is that oftentimes authors who don't understand complex systems or simply don't care try to boil down innumerable factors and conditions into One Weird Trick that brings about salvation and success, that fixes whatever ails you. With Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers it was the idea if you practice 10,000 hours you can generally master some field, or with The Secret it was that if you just yearn for something enough it'll manifest, even if that includes curing cancer or becoming insanely rich. It's universally bullshit for obvious reasons; you'll get better at something if you spend the equivalent of a year-and-a-half straight on it, but there are still going to be limits to your success, while similarly just hoping really hard doesn't force the cosmos to bend to your will. The world is messy, inconsistent, and unique for everyone and everything, and what works for one might not work for another due to forces beyond their control.
Watching Michigan's offense basically every week I've come away with the distinct impression that Jason Beck and co. thought they had that one weird trick in their arsenal that would elevate Michigan's offense to hitherto-unrealized heights. That what worked at New Mexico and Utah, turning the latter into one of the best offenses in the country, would super-charge a team with Michigan's talent in the trenches as well as in the backfield. In the off-season everyone assumed, at worst, that Beck's offensive philosophy would maintain the consistent gap run scheme honed under Sherrone Moore while bolting on a more advanced RPO collection. At best, Harding and Beck would recognize that Michigan had finally successfully implemented stretch as well, which would add yet another further wrinkle and make the QB run game that much more dangerous. And with an established top-end receiver in Marsh being supplemented with a walking mismatch in JJ Buchanan, plus all the TEs and the high-end backs, it felt like a match made in heaven.
But what's become apparent over the weeks is that Beck and co. viewed the offense they inherited as a burden they had to overcome and not a benefit, and seemingly made a point of jettisoning most of it. My general read for a while is that this decision was based in hubris and arrogance, the very clear notion that anything the last guys built was structurally unsound and needed to be replaced by something approved by the current administration. The non-infamous line by Whittingham that "you will become us, we will not become you", in 99th-ranked-offense-in-the-country form.
The problem with any bad offense is that there's not one thing to fix. Changing the QB doesn't eliminate rolling out converted DTs and struggling backup guards to hold up against the rush while sending two receivers out. Trying to run stretch halfway through the year doesn't magically improve block ID'ing by the guards and tackles or improves your QB's middling arm strength. Guys get hurt and their backups prove their behind them for reasons, coaches don't trust throwing in the middle of the field so it's all short slants and outside hitch routes. And the minute defenses adjust to these changes, you're again out of ideas and it's weeks of tinkering to just get back to barely drowning.
So yeah, if anything expect the Rutgers game to be the acme for the offense this year, as UM's incompetence wit the ball was outstripped by the physical manifestation of diminishing Comcast subscribers. If there was a switch to flip or a card to play, even Beck and Whittingham would have used it up by now.
Worst: Paying With Pennies

Way back in the diary around UTEP I noted that the offense lacked explosives like previous seasons (and like Utah had last year). 3 games into the season UM had only 4 plays of 30+ yards and only 1 40+. An offense that can't generate quick strikes, that has to manufacture long drives to score points, is one that can easily be bogged down and inefficient. Having to pick up 6+ first downs every drive puts a lot of strain on everyone both mentally and physically - linemen have to ID defenders each time, your QB has to decode coverages and evade the rush, your RBs need to pick the right hole, etc. Everything is just harder and there are more opportunities for you to screw up, and so that's why "big bills only" offenses tend to be more efficient in aggregate. When the defense fears your RBs and WRs they have adjust to take away the big play, which creates a feedback loop where now they're taking risks you can exploit offensively. When you're an explosive offense, you get on and off the field quickly and put pressure on the defense constantly.
This year Michigan's offense is the person in line who pays for everything with change. They don't have 2 dollar bills but they do have a handful of nickels, dimes, quarters and pennies that they
"know" is more than enough, just let them count it out. In the intervening 6 games since UTEP Michigan's generated 7 plays over 30 yards, 4 over 40 and none beyond that. In fact, Michigan is one of 3 teams to not have a play 50+ yards - the other 2 being Akron and USF. For comparison, Rutgers had 2 50+ yard plays just against Michigan last week and that was with a backup QB and their 1st-round WR barely playing. And from a UM perspective, this is with an offense that features high-level talent at WR, RB, and QB, at least some of which isn't injured and/or being blamed for an OC being a moron. I've said this a lot over the year but it remains inexplicable that Michigan is this colossally bad at getting yards in chunks given just dumb luck; at some point you'd assume a safety would fall down, a RB would break a tackle, something. But no, Michigan's offensive system can't scheme up anything and then even if something big could theoretically break open it fizzles for various reasons.
This inability to matriculate down the field quickly shows up in a lot of stats, from having the 101st-ranked offensive drive success rate (slightly ahead of Rice, Georgia Tech, and this same MSU team) to having an adjusted EPA around where Iowa, UConn, and the Dukies hang out. And if you don't care about rankings, consider the fact UM had 16 3rd-down plays against Rutgers last week on only 9 real-ish drives. I saw people make a big deal about UM converting on 12 of those opportunities but it's not great when you face that many 3rd downs in a game against the 124th-ranked defense in the country. It means you are going on these laborious drives that eat up the clock, shorten the game and limit your opportunities to come back, and put immense pressure to cash in on each opportunity because you can't easily get back to scoring range. Every Michigan TD or FGA drive against the Scarlett Knights was at least 7 plays and 4 of them were 10+. That includes drives of 10-plays, 31 yards and 7 plays, 35 yards.
Against MSU you had fewer long drives due to turnovers, poor game management and incompetence by the coaches, and some cowardly decisions to punt. But even then, Michigan had a 13-play, 71-yard missed FG drive and their lone TD drive was 13 plays and 75 yards against an MSU defense willingly draining the clock up 15. Even that TD drive required a penalty on 4th-and-3 and a 21-yard completion on 4th-and-21 to stay alive, along with various panicked scrambles by Carr. On the day Michigan converted 3 of 11 3rd- and 4-down opportunities compared to MSU's 9-21. Nothing came easy for Michigan all game and that's been the story all season.
And to make matters worse, the last three opponents either have some of the stingiest big-play defenses in the country (UCLA and OSU are both top-12) or Oregon, who've cleaned up the big plays since some early-season struggles. Michigan's longest play from scrimmage against the Spartans was a 4th-and-21 completion to Travis Johnson on a broken play; I'd be amazed if Michigan got more than 1 or 2 20+ plays a game against anyone else on the schedule. So in addition to all the other reasons the Whittingham/Beck marriage has been awful, their inability to not make every drive feel like a deleted scene from The Odyssey.
Worst: Carr Wreck

I've struggled for a while to talk about Tommy Carr as the QB at Michigan because it feels like any criticism of him elicits a "hater" response from a portion of the fanbase. Bryce Underwood's struggles were real but it also felt like a chunk of the fans were angry at him for not being better, that him getting paid a reported $3M/yr. to play football in college was already morally offensive and then he didn't even meet expectations. I'm not going to wade into various other factors I think played a part in certain people clamoring for the backup QB, but before Beck became the focal point of everyone's ire there was a belief that Carr had to play over Underwood because he looked semi-playable in spring ball and it didn't seem possible someone could play worse at QB.
Carr coming in at halftime of the PSU game and benefitting from a couple of short fields, two big runs, and generally playing within himself vindicated the notion that it was Underwood who was the leak in the offense's hull. The Indiana game was predictably bad but had its moments for Carr, and nobody expected him or Underwood to succeed against an elite defense. Then Rutgers came around and Carr performed about how you'd expect a competent college QB would against a terrible defense, flashing poise but also some limitations. But it's hard to argue with 80% completion for 10 ypa.
But in all three games, I kept seeing signs that expecting a true freshman 3.5* QB to be your savior was fool's gold, especially when it came at the expense of a QB with, frankly, much higher upside and a debatably lower downside who's only 1 year older. While Carr could escape the pocket and scramble around, doing so against a terrible Rutgers team wasn't really applicable against anyone else, and his lack of arm strength meant balls that could fit into windows against Rutgers defenders waiting for the PATH train probably wouldn't against better cornerbacks. And even if he was a better intermediate passer, the continued lack of downfield explosives and the limited threat of designed runs meant defenses that were already putting 9 defenders in the box could continue to do so with impunity.
Against MSU Carr really struggled basically from the jump. He seemed a bit amped up (understandable in his first start in a rivalry game), which led to balls sailing and being picked off or airmailed. And as the game progressed, MSU's ability to amp up the pressure on passing downs led to him missing receivers and running into sacks. A lot of these issues were exacerbated by a lack of running game again, something UM fans sorta expected when they couldn't break 4 ypc against Rutgers. But still, it was jarring to see an MSU team down multiple starters on the DL (and really everywhere) manhandle UM on the ground. Yes, Michigan is down to their deep backups at tackle and everyone is hurting, but 54 yards on 26 carries to go along with 5 sacks meant Carr had no pressure release as the game progressed and and, predictably, started freelancing more and running out of protection. And if that feels eerily similar to what Underwood turned into as the year went on, you aren't wrong to notice the similarities. And to make matters worse, at least with Underwood you could involve him in the QB running game and try to escape the pressure; Carr simply isn't that type of athlete right now (and probably won't ever be) and scrambles are something reliable.
What Michigan needed to do to help Carr is what MSU did on that 17-play, 79-yard FG drive that started at their 1. Outside of a couple of passes, they leaned on their running backs to just keep pushing against UM's defense, picking up enough yards to keep Michigan guessing defensively and not put too much on Milivojevic's shoulders. And they did it mostly running split zone with some wrinkles thrown in; simple stuff that is in Michigan's playbook and well within their abilities to execute, one assumes. Mind you, this was also accomplished with their 3rd and 4th-string RBs and a patchwork OL. But Michigan never gave Carr much of a chance, burning early downs with short gains out of obvious formations and then asking him to run around and make plays that he couldn't realistically do.
In the end Carr's stat line was 14/26 for 138 yards and 2 picks. And honestly, it was uglier than that as he picked up 60 yards on the final drive when he broke the pocket a number of times and his receivers made some great plays/MSU's general incompetence on defense broke thru despite their best efforts. You can see the upside for Carr but there's no reason he should be playing now.
I don't know if any of the past 4 games turn out differently with Underwood under center (Seth mentioned in the Rutgers podcast Carr wins that while Underwood loses it and I'm going to need to see the work behind that claim), but this felt like a game where too much was put on the shoulders of Carr and he struggled mightily as a result. The stuff he was supposedly good at (providing a credible passing threat) didn't materialize and there wasn't any other pitches in the arsenal. With Underwood you'd at least have potential QB runs and the attendant optionality, plus you'd be able to run your QB in short-yardage situations instead of putting a fucking big red "come tackle our QB who's definitely throwing the ball" on a crucial 2-point conversion try when you send your RB out to the boundary and leave an empty backfield.
Meh: 15 Points Should Be Enough
This is going to be short because I'm sort of tired of the both-sidesing by some around the offense and defense on this team. Did Michigan's defense give up yards due to some poor tackling and missed assignments that allowed MSU to keep drives alive? Yes. Did they have yet another epic drive by an opponent that was mostly dinks-and-dunks? Sure. Did it basically feel like Minnesota part deux at times? Absolutely.
But at the end of the day, Michigan gave up 5 FGs and under 300 yards of total offense despite being on the field for nearly 80 plays compared to UM's 52. They gave up 4 ypp on the day, which isn't great against MSU but not some spectacular failure. In the end, 15 points given up against Sparty should be more than enough to win a game in 2026. Case in point - this skeet pointed out that Michigan hasn't given 21 points all year in their first 9 games, a feat accomplished only 14 other times since 2011. Over that period, those other 14 teams are a combined 119-7, while Michigan is 5-4.
A defense can't be perfect, and even the 2023 unit could have down drives. This defense has flaws but it's insane how much the offense has wasted what is a championship-level unit across the field, and I hope fans enjoy it because given the upcoming attrition my guess is we won't be seeing something like this in the future for a while.
Quick Hits:
On the long list of dumb shit Whittingham and co. have done this year, having freshman Jacob Bagget come out to take the first FG of his career in a rivalry game and then still have Butkowski squib the onside kick cold is up there. Maybe hiring guys like Coombs and Whittingham, who are quite friendly with Urban Meyer and other members of your most hated rival, was a bad idea because, you know, they might suck at their jobs and make your worse.
The receivers were fine, I guess, by Marsh had another fumble and it feels like everyone is sorta checked out. Carr threw some ducks that forced Buchanan and Marsh to play defense, and it sure feels like Travis Johnson is going to be WR1 after everyone else leaves and that's not a great feeling.
Even with the fumble at least Kuzdzal was able to gain yards at times against this awful defense. He could have gone to a bunch of G5 programs and gotten starter carries; it sucks he came back only to see the guys ahead of him struggle this much. If Harding now calling the plays I hope they settle on a main back whether it be Hitter or Kuzdzal and ride him out.
Next Week: Oregon
I was seriously calling this column the end of the season, but with Beck out at OC I'm intrigued enough to see what next week brings. Oregon is on the outskirts of the playoff picture after some early losses and Moore getting knocked out for the year but they've rebounded on offense with Raiola under center and a new OC and their defense remains really good. They just curb-stomped OSU and my guess is they'll do the same to Michigan in the end, but UM's defense should put up a decent fight for a while. And hell, maybe UM will just run a normal offense with normal plays and put their best players out there and see what happens. UM is going to lose but my hope is they show...something with the switch.

msu.headline: Soccer Teams See Mixed Results On Sunday
msu.body:
Michigan State’s head coach Jeff Hosler, center, talks with the team during the first half in the game against Loyola on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, at DeMartin Stadium in East Lansing. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

I know Spartan Nation is still basking in the glow of last night’s football victory.  Today, we had more teams playing in big games.  Both the Men’s and Women’s Soccer Teams had Big Ten Tournament games today.  The earlier game was the men’s quarterfinal matchup against Maryland, where the Spartans were the 4-seed and the Terrapins were the 5-seed.  An hour later, the women, also seeded 4th, had a semifinal against 8-seed um.

The Men’s Team ended up falling in their game, losing 2-1.  Maryland took a 1-0 lead in the 33rd minute and then doubled the advantage early in the 2nd half to take control.  The Spartans only cracked the scoreboard in the 88th minute but were unable to get an equalizer before the buzzer.  Now they will have to wait to see if they earn a spot in the NCAA Tournament.  The selection show will be on November 16.

The Women’s Team had a better result than the men, and for the second straight day, the Spartans beat the wolverines.  The game’s lone goal came on a free kick in the 40th minute from just outside the box.  Defensewoman Renee Watson took the kick and bent it just over the wall of defenders and into the back of the net before um’s goalie could dive for it.

Left-footed shot curls into the right corner for Renee Watson gives us the first-half lead. pic.twitter.com/xzU5oVHk9V
— Michigan State Women's Soccer (@MSU_wsoccer) November 8, 2026

The Lady Spartans will play for the Big Ten Championship on Friday against the winner of the Purdue/Wisconsin semifinal.  If Wisconsin wins, the final will be in East Lansing, but Purdue will host the championship game if they take down the Badgers.

msu.headline: Sun Finally Shines as MSU Downs Michigan in The Weather Report
msu.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 07: Nick Sharpe #52 of the Michigan State Spartans and the Michigan State Spartans mascot celebrate with the Paul Bunyan Trophy after a 15-6 win over the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Holy expletive! Doth my eyes deceive me? Is this truly an MSU victory? Over the weasels? In their play pen? The answer is yes, yes to all of it. It has been a rough season without a doubt, but to beat Michigan, that is a game all of us would be happy to win. So, we finally have ourselves some real joy for this week’s weather report.

Sun #1

The first sun has to go to Joe Rossi. I mean the man barely has people available to take the field. The defense looked prepared, had a game plan, and executed. Five sacks, four turnovers and a near shutout all against your rival on the road without half of your normal starters is exactly why Rossi gets the sun. Plus the batted down passes, and tackle for losses just added to the reasoning. I loved the intensity and physicality of the defense. The defense has been gritty all year. Not always successful, but they’ve been gritty. They have had a grit that is what Spartan football is supposed to be. This was a special win and this defense deserves a lot of that credit. Now the question is, can a win like this give this team a push for the rest of the season?

Sun #2

My second sun is headed to the kicking game. First and foremost, Liam Boyd was lights out. Every kick mattered and he was as solid as someone could be. The 49 yarder, that could have been good for longer, was a nail in the coffin kick. Boyd wasn’t the only boot that made a difference. Rhys Dakin had some great punts. Only had to punt four times but three of them were inside the 20. That just allowed the defense more opportunity to tee up on the weasels. Let’s also not forget to give a shout out to Jacob Baggett for his beautiful doink off the upright. It was little things like that that gave me hope that we had a chance. Second time this season I’m handing out a sun to Liam Boyd.

Sun #3

I have a shared third sun. My first part is going to the stat sheet and MSU dominating in everything. Time of possession, passing, rushing, turnovers, and as usual against Michigan, penalties. It was a strange feeling to feel there was this chance all game long. Our memory of Northwestern and Illinois made it difficult to keep the hope but ultimately, MSU was in charge this whole game. Part two of this shared sun is going to the booing Michigan fans. There is nothing I love more that hearing weasel fans boo their own team, in their own house. Boo away Ann Arbor, boo your way through all your excuses.

Cloud #1

First cloud goes to the inability to punch it in the end zone. Michigan has a solid defense and one that showed that as it shut MSU out of the end zone for the whole game. MSU was close numerous times but never could cross the line. The Spartans have got to get the ball in the end zone when you get that close. Some of the problem was play calling and some was just being outplayed. Thankfully, MSU still managed to put points up with the field goals.

Cloud #2

Cloud 2 is headed to the 7 penalties because I can finally be a bit picky with the clouds. You have to expect the whistles when playing in the play pen and the 7 penalties were not good. Honestly though, it is hard to make this a cloud because MSU was playing physical and typically would have been called for even more. I’m glad they were getting hands on receivers and fortunate the interference calls or even phantom late hit calls weren’t called to benefit the weasels. So, this is like a half cloud, which leads me to my next conundrum.

Cloud #3…nah Sun #4

I’m sorry my friends but I am too elated to talk negative and my hatred for the opponent has been at unhealthy levels since childhood. So, let’s talk about some more sun. I want to mention some individuals who helped this win. Shout out to Alessio for getting on the field after being questionable all week. Shout out to Chrishon McCray for some big time catches to keep things moving and momentum staying with Sparta. Shout out to Brandon Tullis who had 25 carries for 86 yards. There were not many of those 86 yards that came easy, but he continued to push and at times get just enough. Lastly, a shout out to Coach Fitz. The final score has not always been in our favor but the grit, the handling of adversity, the effort being made to get back to what Spartan football is has been noticed. I know there are plenty that don’t want him here and hated the hire. I think after the way this team has fought each week through all of its adversities is a testament to your coach and I think Fitz deserves some credit for that and a bit of grace.

Well, let’s hear it TOC, I want to see those suns and clouds in the comments. Before you do though, can we just take a moment to breathe in, smile, give a little laugh that we managed to beat Michigan coming into the game on a 6 game losing streak? Please make sure you irritate every weasel you see this week, especially the Walmart ones, because even with the loaded excuses that are sure to pour out, Paul is still going to be back where he belongs. Go Green!

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State Takes Down um, 15-6
msu.body:
Nov 7, 2026; Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; Michigan State Spartans wide receiver Chrishon McCray (13) runs the ball against the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rick Osentoski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

From early on in this game, and as many people already knew, it was clear that this was a game between two not good teams.  Unfortunately for us Spartan fans, we have had a couple unlucky breaks while tonight’s opponent has had some good fortune in their season.  Watching the two teams in the first half, one would imagine their records were closer than the reality.

Michigan State got the ball first and moved the chains one time before punting.

On their first defensive stand, Michigan State got a turnover when safety Devin Vaught came down with a pick after a pass went off an um receiver’s finger tips.

Starting a yard inside um territory, the Spartans reached 4th & 2 on the first series.  Coach Fitzgerald decided to be aggressive, and the play call was for a deep shot.  Personally, I would have rather punted here to try pinning an unimpressive offense deep.  Predictably, the deep shot did not pay off.  Receiver Bryson Williams had a chance at it but dropped the pass.

The two teams traded punts on their next possessions, totaling 17 yards of offense between them.  On um’s ensuing drive, they had their best drive of the half, moving 71 yards in 13 plays over six and a half minutes.  They reached the MSU 7, but a 3rd & 1 run lost a yard and brought out the field goal unit.  The kick went off the near side upright and bounced out, keeping the game with no points on the board.

Again, the two teams traded punts.  Getting the ball right at the 50, the Spartans marched all the way to the 3-yard line before having to settle for a field goal, which Liam Boyd made.  Just like that, the Spartans were ahead.

MSU then forced a 3-and-out.  Chrishon McCray muffed the punt reception but retrieved the fumble, and MSU took over at their own 44.  MSU picked up a couple first downs, the second on a 35-yard pass to McCray that got the Spartans down to the 13.  A bogus offensive pass interference penalty in the endzone pushed MSU back near the 20 and eventually led to another FG try, which Boyd comfortably made.

There was only time for a kneel-down after the kickoff, and MSU took a 6-0 lead to the break.  Our defense only gave up 78 total yards through two quarters.

MSU started the second half on defense, and after giving up a first down on the first play, forced a punt.  Unfortunately for us, that punt was allowed to land and it flatlined at the 1-yard line, pinning Alessio Milivojevic and the MSU offense against the goalline.

Starting from the 1-yard line, Michigan State had, perhaps, their most impressive drive since week 2.  The Spartans held the ball for 10:41 of game clock, ran 17 plays, and picked up 6 first downs.  There were passes, runs, wildcats, and overall dominance from MSU.  After reaching the um 12, the offense finally came to a halt with a run for a loss and then a sack.  Liam Boyd came on and hit his 3rd field goal, this one from 38 yards, to put MSU up 9-0.

On um’s ensuing drive, the referees started trying to help the home team.  After it looked like MSU was going to force a 3-and-out, a penalty was called for “illegal substitution” because an MSU defender had the heel of his shoe still on the field when the ball was snapped.  So um got another crack at a 3rd down play, on which MSU was called for pass interference (after a called reception was overturned).  On the next play, um ran the ball through the middle of the Spartan defense, but Lafaele punched the ball out late and Nikai Martinez recovered the loose ball.  Of course, after the play, MSU was penalized 15 yards for celebrating.

After a 28-yard catch-and-run by Chrishon McCray, MSU went backwards for a few plays and ended up punting, but Rhys Dakin pinned um at their own 7 with 12:01 to play.

After giving up a first down to start the drive, the Spartan defense then tackled um for a loss of a yard on a running play, followed that up with a sack by Derrick Simmons, and then got an interception from NiJhay Burt on a deep shot at the MSU 38.

Back on offense, the highlight of the drive was a 36-yard play to Bryson Williams.  The drive lasted 10 plays and over 5 minutes of game clock, and ended in Boyd’s fourth field goal to put MSU up 12-0.

With just over 5 minutes left, um needed to do something quick.  Instead, they held the ball for two plays, fumbling at their 37-yard line after a catch.  NiJhay Burt forced and recovered the fumble.

The Spartans ran the ball three times, then brought Boyd on to hit a 49-yard kick for a 15-0 lead.

The MSU defense then forced a turnover on downs on the first series of um’s possession… but a pass interference gave um an extra life.  After two incompletions and an 11-yard sack, MSU surrendered a 22-yard pass on 4th down.  An 11-yard run moved the chains again for um.  Two plays later, they hit a 31-yard pass to the 1, and then scored a play later to ruin the Spartan shutout.  Now trailing 15-6, um elected to go for two, but Kenny Soares shut that down with an amazing spin move to get home for the sack.

The kickoff was an obvious onside attempt, but the ball only went 6 yards before hitting an um player, giving MSU the ball.  Three kneeldowns later, it was game over and VICTORY FOR MSU!!!!

Sure, it would have been even sweeter to get the shutout, but this was still a dominant win against our rival in a game no one, including myself and many here among TOC Nation, was really giving us much of a chance to win.  For the game, MSU outgained um 298-192 and controlled the clock with over 38 minutes of possession.  The defense created four turnovers.  As Pat Fitzgerald said after the game, “Paul Bunyan is coming home to East Lansing!”

While it can still be said that this was a game between two not good teams, it is clear that um is much more not good than MSU.

tigers.headline: RHP Dustin May may fit the Tigers’ needs for starting pitching depth
tigers.body:
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 27: Dustin May #21 of the Milwaukee Brewers throws a pitch during the first inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in game four of the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on October 27, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the near certainty of a lockout and a long fight between players and owners this offseason, it’s hard to get real enthusiastic about free agency right now. It’s usually hard for Tigers’ fans in the first place. While there is the idea being floated that top free agent Tarik Skubal may sign before the December 1st lockout if the right offer is available, with the Dodgers, Mets, and Cubs, generally regarded as his main suitors, he’s a pretty unique case. Apart from Skubal, there seems to be widespread expectation that most free agents will wait until new terms of the next collective bargaining agreement are announced before signing. Likewise, teams need to know the payroll constraints they’ll be working under to really manage their budget for free agents.

However, there’s also likely to be a set of moves from many teams simply designed to shore up depth where possible before the lockout begins. Scott Harris has a habit of trying to add a depth starter early in the offseason. These moves have generally gone pretty poorly, although Drew Anderson was a better choice last year than most. Even so, Harris certainly seems to emphasize getting a little depth in his offseason shopping early on, perhaps with the idea that he won’t have to force a move later. This strategy has not worked out terribly well, but that’s more been a matter of picking the wrong pitchers. The theory is still reasonably sound, particularly with the lockout looming. I wouldn’t be surprised to see him try it again.

The Tigers have a pretty solid group to build a rotation out of next season, but they aren’t necessarily that deep either. By 2028 the Tigers may have a pretty good crop of starting pitching prospects in the upper minors. Right now, they do not. And as we’ve discussed repeatedly since the regular season ended, the Tigers need for high leverage relievers is best answered by converting 1-2 of their starters with big stuff, but limited recent workloads, into relief help. To do that they’re going to need to pick up another starting option this offseason.

The criteria is pretty simple. We’re just looking at short term deals here. The Tigers are highly unlikely to go after a big target in the starting pitching market. National media is going to continue to report that the Tigers are “keeping tabs” on the Tarik Skubal market, but no one is buying that as long as the reported price tag remains well over $300 million. The Tigers will be angling for depth here unless Scott Harris decides to break his usual patterns, so it’s not going to be a thrilling signing when and if they add an arm. Deciding to lock up a decidedly mediocre journeyman reliever in Jacob Waguespack should probably be seen as the corollary to any depth starter signing that could come before the lockout begins.

Let’s take a look at Dustin May, who is a pretty good all around fit for what the Tigers will probably look for in a free agent starter.

RHP Dustin May

SeasonIPERAFIPK%BB%HR/9fWAR2025132.14.964.8821.19.61.430.72026145.24.703.6323.28.10.862.8

This veteran right-hander makes some sense for the Tigers. The lanky 29-year-old has never been able to translate his velocity into high-end whiff rates, and his breaking stuff has never carved hitters up the way many expected when he was a prospect. On the other hand, he’s fairly consistent and took a notable leap in preventing home runs this season while finally putting his years in injury purgatory behind him.

Between 2021-2024, when he was still with the Dodgers, May’s career was in shambles as he had two UCL reconstruction surgeries with just a brief comeback in between them. He was still effective in his brief stints on the mound, but his early potential was going to waste as his mid-20’s were largely spent on the injured list. He was traded to the Boston Red Sox at the deadline in 2025. The Cardinals signed him to a one-year deal worth $12.5M for 2026 before they dealt him to the World Series champs back at the trade deadline. For two seasons now he’s been generally healthy, throwing 132.1 and 145.2 innings the past two seasons, with no major injury trouble.

May is still averaging just shy of 97 mph on his fourseam and sinker with a bit more than average extension. He’s largely backing that with his 93-94 mph cutter in a very fastball heavy profile. He uses his 86 mph sweeper a decent amount, but the break on that is a little too big to fool major league hitters as much as the movement might predict. May rips his 86 mph sweeper at over 3000 rpms, and late in the season, he started throwing more of a straight curveball at 83.7 mph, with the same monstrous spin rate and getting more whiffs with it. We didn’t see it working as effectively in the postseason. In general, May gets a very balanced spread of grounders, line drives, and fly balls, so he’s fairly neutral in terms of how park factors will affect him.

He still feels to me like a guy who might be better off ditching the cutter and trying to throw more of a prototypical slider instead, while continuing to experiment with the sweeper/curveball combo as more of a strike stealer that is hard to square up for lefties. Sometimes throwing cutters, fourseamers, and sinkers all can diminish each of those pitches individually by requiring some fairly subtle feel differences how they’re gripped and released.

However, May was with the Dodgers a long time, so I would guess there have been plenty of stuff experiments under smart coaches along the way. The intriguing note for me was his increased curveball usage late in the year and the velocity on that pitch. Both Jackson Jobe and Beau Brieske started ripping an 85-86 mph curveball that neither had really thrown before, and the pitch looked pretty whiffish in the brief looks we had of them. Possibly the Brewers were thinking along similar lines with May, making this a little more interesting fit in Detroit.

May intrigues me to a degree is that he’s missed a lot of time in his career and really hasn’t had long stretches of good health in which to actually hone his craft and get better. Of course, you can just as easily call that being injury prone, but you take a look at May’s raw stuff and the wildly varying arm angles from year to year, it feels like he’s still tinkering for the right arm angle and stuff.

The Tigers don’t really need a workhorse here. May just completed back-to-back full seasons for the first time in his major league career, and yet he’s been with four teams over those two seasons. He hasn’t had a chance to settle in anywhere. And yet, May had a pretty good first half before fading as the season progressed. His 4.38 ERA with the Cardinals was solid, and he boasted a 3.15 FIP in St. Louis that said he’d actually been somewhat unlucky. He dealt with back tightness in June and then an ankle contusion in July, and really wasn’t pitching well through that stretch.

May briefly got off to a good start in Milwaukee, but blew up in a start on August 19th and the next time out took a 106 mph liner to his back, striking him in the upper back on the right side. He struggled the rest of the way, posting an ERA of 5.65 with the Brewers as they limited his starts and kept a quick hook on him. He was okay in the postseason, but again was working short outings with a mix of starts and relief appearances after an opener.

May dominates right-handed hitters. His trouble has always been allowing power and walks to lefties. In 2026, the problem was really just those walks. The Tigers being in pretty good shape with lefty relievers says that May would have a quick hook hanging over him in the middle innings of any start where a tough pocket of lefties was coming up in the opposing lineup.

Things are set up pretty well for May to have a solid season in 2027. I wouldn’t expect much more than 125-145 innings, but his production should be basically league average or a little better. He would be the Tigers’ fifth starter, and might get flexed into middle relief work here and there as well. That would allow the Tigers to use one of River Ryan, Troy Melton, or Keider Montero in high leverage roles along with Drew Sommers and hopefully, Will Vest next year. If Reese Olson is finally healthy, that opens up more options.

I’m not convinced that May has tons of upside remaining or anything, but his velocity and ability to spin the baseball will continue to intrigue teams around the league. The Tigers would be happy with his Cardinals production during most of the 2026 season, and hope to help him be more consistent from start to start and cut down on the walks to lefties. Solid depth starter work with some flexibility would do just fine, though he’ll likely be angling for a two-year deal after proving that he’s finally beyond all the elbow troubles.

MLB Trade Rumors projects a two-year, $30M deal with a player opt-out after year one. Like most contracts of this type, you’re rarely going to love it, but it might be just what the Tigers need to allow them to focus on the bullpen.

tigers.headline: Tigers announce 2027 coaching and training staff
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 17: Manager A.J. Hinch #14 of the Detroit Tigers looks on against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 17, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Tigers confirmed recent reports on hirings for their 2027 coaching staff on Friday. They announced the hiring of Kyle Hudson as the new first base and baserunning coach. Hudson worked with outfielders in his most recent job as Boston Red Sox’s third base coach, so perhaps he’ll take on some of those responsibilities in Detroit as well. Still the emphasis from the Tigers is on the baserunning side. Hudson was also an assistant coach for the Cleveland Guardians from 2020-2022 before joining the Red Sox.

The Tigers had already hired longtime major league catcher Martin Maldonado, whom AJ Hinch worked with briefly in Houston, as their new quality coach this offseason. Maldonado was behind the plate during the Astros 2022 run to the World Series championship. He brings a strong reputation as a leader and game planner, as well as his skill coaching the position, to the Tigers.

Longtime catching coach Ryan Sienko, who joined the organization in 2021, AJ Hinch’s first year as manager, will retain his duties coaching catchers, but will also now handle duties as bullpen coach following Juan Nieves departure from the organization. It’s typically a pitching coach in that role, so that’s a bit interesting. Presumably, Maldonado will handle more of the pre-game pitch planning with Dillon Dingler and Eduardo Valencia, while Sienko will continue coaching the actual catching skills, but perhaps their responsibilities will be mixed between them as well.

The Tigers have yet to replace Gabe Ribas as director of pitching in the farm system after his departure to work for the Colorado Rockies last offseason. They’ve replaced Nieves, who has been Chris Fetter’s assistant pitching coach since 2021, with a catcher, leaving Fetter and assistant Robin Lund as a duo to coach the pitchers. Perhaps they’ll end up hiring a new pitching director this offseason, but it’s a bit peculiar that they’re cutting out both major and minor league pitching coaches. Those responsibilities still have to be fulfilled by someone, but without some detailed clarification from the organization it’s difficult to pin down who is actually doing what at this point in regard to those roles.

The Tigers have named Kyle Hudson as their major league first base and baserunning coach.

Martin Maldonado has been named major league quality coach.

Hudson and Maldonado join manager A.J. Hinch’s coaching staff that otherwise returns intact from the end of the 2026 campaign,…
— Tigers PR (@DetroitTigersPR) November 6, 2026

George Lombard is expected to stay on for his seventh year as Tigers bench coach under Hinch. Billy Boyer took over from Joey Cora as third base coach during the 2026 season and seems set to remain in that role. Beyond Maldonado, Hudson, Sienko, Fetter, and Lund, the Tigers are working with a three-man group of hitting coaches. Michael Brdar, Cody Asche, and Lance Zawadski, who seem set to be retained for 2027. Boyer was the Tigers quality control coach last season, and will cede that job to Maldonado.

Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic also reports that the Tigers have hired Scott Peters as their new medical director, while Jeremiah Randle has been hired as the Tigers new athletic trainer. Peters was most recently the director of health and performance science for the Toronto Blue Jays. Randall was the head athletic trainer for the Astros from 2016-2025.

Former head trainer Ryan Eubanks and assistent trainer Chris McDonald parted ways with the Tigers organization at season’s end.

The Tigers also confirmed the hiring of Jay Sartori as Vice President of Baseball Operations. Sartori was formerly an assistant general manager in the organization going back to the beginning of the Tigers rebuild in 2017. He left last season for a college job in the ACC but has returned to the fold this offseason.

The Tigers have finalized their 2027 coaching staff. Kyle Hudson and Martín Maldonado are the only new additions. Ryan Sienko becomes bullpen coach in addition to his duties as catching coach.

Scott Peters is the new medical director. Jeremiah Randall is head athletic trainer.
